extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (trademark attorneys and trademark agents), respondents in OED disciplinary proceedings, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing practitioner conduct in USPTO trademark matters, especially electronic-signature rules, duties to cooperate with OED investigations, and the consequences/process for exclusion on consent and reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic signature requirements for trademark filings (37 C.F.R. § 2.193)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence that requires a signature filed with the USPTO in trademark matters must bear: (1) a handwritten signature personally signed in permanent ink by the person named as the signatory, or a true copy thereof; or (2) an electronic signature that meets the requirements of paragraph (c) of this section, personally entered by the person named as the signatory. The Office will accept an electronic signature ... through TEAS or ESTTA. A person signing a document electronically must personally enter the characters that he or she has adopted as their signature, placed between two forward slash symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default TEAS sign method is 'DIRECT' where the applicant personally enters the characters adopted as their signature. Other methods include 'E SIGN-ON' (link sent to third party who signs directly) and 'H SIGN-ON' (upload of electronic version of original handwritten signature). Typing another person's electronic signature is not a valid signature. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a),(c) and TMEP § 611.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP signature guidance (TMEP § 611.01(b)–(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP § 611.01 sets forth general and specific requirements for signatures of trademark documents filed with the Office, including that all documents must be personally signed, that the person identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature, and that another person (paralegal, legal assistant, secretary) may not sign the name of an attorney or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP explicitly states 'typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person.' Practitioners and representatives should consult the TMEP (available online) for practice and procedural references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on others signing for the signatory (In re Dermahose; In re Cowan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, secretary) may not sign the name of an attorney or other authorized signatory on trademark filings; signing the name of another person on paper or typing another person's electronic signature does not serve as that person's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permit staff or third parties to enter the signatory's signature characters; use proper E SIGN-ON or H SIGN-ON procedures if another's direct entry is required and permitted by rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of signature integrity (declarations under 18 U.S.C. § 1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signature requirements are critical because each application includes a declaration required to be signed by the person whose name appears as signatory, and the declaration contains certifications signed under criminal penalty of fine or imprisonment pursuant to 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper signatures risk criminally-significant false statements and undermine the integrity of the trademark registration process; practitioners must ensure truthful, properly-made declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS/TICRS audit trail and IP evidence (TICRS captures signature method and IP address)
rubrics_metrics.description: TICRS captures and records when a document is created on TEAS, when it is submitted, and the signature method used; TICRS also records the IP address of the computer used by the document preparer to access TEAS. When 'DIRECT' is used, the IP address routinely specifies geographic location of the computer used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TICRS and TEAS audit trail (timestamps, signature method, IP address/geolocation) can be used as evidence of who actually entered a signature and where filings were prepared; practitioners should be aware such metadata is recorded and review internal processes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner duty to cooperate with OED investigations (37 C.F.R. § 11.22 and § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: During an investigation, OED may request information and evidence pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(t)(1)(ii). A practitioner has an ethical obligation to respond to any lawfully issued Request for Information; 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) proscribes knowingly failing to respond to a request from OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly to RFIs within the stated deadline or seek extensions; failure to respond by the due date can result in a Lack of Response letter, adverse inferences, and disciplinary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse inference and consequences for failing to respond to RFI
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practitioner does not respond to a timely, lawfully issued RFI from OED, 'an adverse inference could be drawn' from the failure to respond, and the failure itself can be charged as professional misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-response is actionable; practitioners should preserve records of responses and communications and treat RFIs seriously to avoid inference of culpability or separate misconduct charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: failure to provide competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to fail to provide competent representation to a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain competence in handling trademark matters, including proper filing procedures and adherence to USPTO rules; negligence or willful omissions that harm clients may constitute misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering another person's signature or otherwise misrepresenting who signed a document can constitute dishonesty/fraud and lead to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper signature practices or failing to cooperate with investigations may be treated as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not explicitly covered elsewhere, conduct undermining public trust or the practitioner's reliability before the Office can trigger discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED authority to approve affidavit of resignation and exclude on consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.27; 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D), 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. § 11.27, the USPTO Director has authority to approve an Affidavit of Resignation and to exclude a practitioner on consent from practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Affidavit of Resignation submitted during a pending disciplinary complaint may be approved, resulting in exclusion on consent; the affidavit must comply with the requirements of § 11.27(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of exclusion on consent on reinstatement (37 C.F.R. § 11.60 presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: By consenting to exclusion while a disciplinary complaint is pending, the respondent acknowledged that if and when she applies for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 the OED Director will conclusively presume, for the purpose of determining the application for reinstatement, that (a) the allegations in the disciplinary complaint are true, and (b) she could not have successfully defended herself against such allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consenting to exclusion has long-term consequences: future reinstatement applications will be adjudicated against the presumption that the underlying allegations are true unless the rules provide otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirements for disciplinary orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at the OED electronic FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette 'materially consistent' with the provided Notice of Exclusion on Consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary actions and exclusions are public; practitioners should expect public posting of orders and a public notice describing the basis for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations following exclusion: compliance with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall comply fully with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 and shall comply fully with 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 upon any request for reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Final Order does not restate § 11.58, the order imposes a duty to follow statutory/regulatory obligations after exclusion (e.g., client notification, file transfer, other administrative duties specified in the cited provisions) and to adhere to reinstatement procedures under § 11.60.
